tob-10036: Delivered as the prestigious Bampton Lectures at Oxford, William Ralph Inge’s survey traces the history of Christian mysticism from the early church through the Middle Ages. He examines thinkers who sought direct union with God and asks what their experiences mean for modern faith. Inge, who later became Dean of St Paul’s, wrote with a rare mix of scholarly depth and readable prose.
tob-10236: The Lotus Sutra is among the most influential scriptures in all of Buddhism, beloved across East Asia for nearly two thousand years. Through parables — a burning house, a lost son, a rain that falls on all plants alike — it teaches that every being carries the seed of Buddhahood. W. E. Soothill’s translation follows the classic Chinese version by Kumarajiva.
tob-10836: Before he became James I of England, the Scottish king wrote this treatise on witchcraft and demons, prompted by the witch trials of his reign. In dialogue form he argues that witches truly exist and must be punished, drawing on scripture and classical sources. The book helped fuel the witch-hunting fever of the early modern age.
tob-13136: Behind the anonymous name ‘Three Initiates’ lies a concise statement of Hermetic philosophy, organized around seven laws governing the universe — the principle of mind, of cause and effect, of gender, and more. Published in 1908, it translated lofty occult ideas into plain, practical language. The Kybalion became one of the best-selling guides to Western esotericism.
tob-13736: Theosophists Annie Besant and Charles Leadbeater claimed the rare ability to see thoughts as shapes and colors in the spiritual atmosphere. This book illustrates their visions — what anger, devotion, or music ‘looks like’ to the clairvoyant eye — in vivid color plates. Part occult manual, part art book, it became a cult classic of the esoteric world.
tob-0036: The Air Force’s 1997 report gives the official word on Roswell — the 1947 wreckage came of Project Mogul, a hush-hush balloon train built to overhear Soviet bomb tests. It accounts for the debris, the ‘bodies,’ and the long rumor-tail. Whether it shuts the case, readers must judge.
tob-4136: Waite’s Secret Tradition in Freemasonry holds the craft sprung from olden mystery schools — a daring say for 1911. This opening volume tracks the veiled teaching through Masonry’s long story, rite by rite. His vast learning makes it gripping reading. Even doubters will find riches here.
tob-4236: John Burnet’s Early Greek Thought tracks the fore-runners — Thales to Democritus — with scholar’s care and clearness. His work set the English standard for the first thinkers. The book made thought’s beginnings open to all. A classic of classic scholarship.
tob-13336: Swami Vivekananda’s How to Be a God-Seeker strings his plain workmanlike teachings — on stillness, breath-taming, and the ordered life. The swami’s rede bore yoga within western readers’ reach. His words still steady beginners today. The book stays a clear first guide to practice.
cia-0000112336: An August 1990 report — title carrying the archive's typos — on TASS planning to publish a bulletin on mysterious phenomena. The Soviet press was opening up to UFOs, psychics, and the paranormal as glasnost loosened controls. The CIA noted it all, filing the strange alongside the strategic.
cia-0000112836: A November 1945 interview with Morris Levitsky, a man of many aliases — Maurice, Levitske, Levit, and more. Multiple names meant multiple lives, and intelligence officers wanted to know about all of them. The entry is a case file on identity itself: who was this man, really?
cia-0000119736: An Eastern Europe briefing on the Hungarian situation from September 1956. Hungary's unrest was read alongside Poland's — two satellites testing the limits at once. The document shows the bloc-wide view: not one crisis, but a system under strain.

un-ga-res-36: Resolution 36 of the General Assembly, adopted in 1946. The founders could not have imagined the institution their votes would become. The catalog preserves the number and date; the resolution preserves their decision.
un-ga-res-3236: General Assembly Resolution 3236, adopted in November 1974 — the landmark text reaffirming the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people, including self-determination and the right of return. Passed as the PLO gained international standing, it became the legal cornerstone of the Palestinian cause at the UN. The resolution is the affirmation: the rights, declared.

un-sc-res-1736: Security Council Resolution 1736, adopted in 2006 — aligned. The mid-2000s Council at work. The number and year endure; the decision is in the text.
cia-0000136636: A 1961 CIA file of Spanish-text 2506 Brigade documents — number 0000136636. The brigade's Spanish record, another installment. The entry is the installment: the record, continued.

un-sc-res-736: Security Council Resolution 736, adopted in 1992 — aligned. The new-members year's Council. The designation and year endure; the act is in the text.

frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d336: The Assistant Secretary of War McCloy to the Secretary of War Stimson — the truncated title cuts off the rest — Document 336. Another internal memo. The memo is the second: McCloy, again.

arxiv-2605-08936: A reasoning model can wander down an unsafe chain of thought before it ever produces an answer. Dongcheng Zhang, Yi Zhang, Yuxin Chen, and colleagues teach models to self-recover: Self-ReSET detects unsafe reasoning trajectories mid-stream and steers back to safety. The 2026 paper is AI safety that watches the thinking, not just the final words.
arxiv-2605-09436: Glasses vibrate oddly: the boson peak — an excess of low-frequency vibrations — has puzzled physicists for decades. Cunyuan Jiang traces its microscopic origin in amorphous solids, down to the atomic arrangements responsible. The 2026 paper is condensed-matter physics on a fifty-year mystery.
arxiv-2605-09736: Quantum fields in de Sitter space suffer infrared divergences — long-wavelength trouble that will not go away. Alexander Kamenshchik, Polina Petriakova, and Tereza Vardanyan tame them with autonomous equations, stochastic methods, and Borel resummation. The 2026 paper is cosmology's quantum underbelly.
arxiv-2605-10036: 6G agentic AI-RAN — radio networks with AI agents — needs a unified memory paradigm to bridge the cognitive gap. Xijun Wang, Zhaoyang Liu, Chenyuan Feng, and colleagues propose it. The 2026 paper is next-generation networks with shared memory. It unifies memory for 6G agents.
plos-pone-0003436: Conservation biologists read the history of a Mexican forest in this 2008 paper. By mapping where species of the tropical dry forest diversified, the authors distinguished sources that export new species from sinks that merely receive them. Those source areas became conservation priorities, since protecting them safeguards the engine of future biodiversity.
plos-pone-0003536: Psychologists found angry faces stick in the mind in this 2008 fMRI study. Volunteers held faces in visual short-term memory, and angry expressions were remembered better than neutral ones. Brain scans revealed the neural correlates of that advantage, showing how emotion tunes the social memory we rely on every day.
plos-pone-0003636: Geneticists Catano, Kulkarni, and He chased HIV's genetic brakes to their source in this 2008 paper. Effects previously credited to the ZNRD1, HCP5, and HLA-C regions were re-examined, with the protective signal traced mainly to specific alleles. The fine-mapping sharpens the hunt for the human variants that slow HIV.
plos-pone-0003736: In 2008, Hong and Dawid found a blood protein building fish livers. Alpha2 macroglobulin-like, a relative of a well-known blood protein, proved essential for liver development in zebrafish. The surprise role gives a familiar molecule a new job in organ building.
plos-pone-0003836: In 2008, Irwin and Finkel mined ocean data for the rules of green seas. Sifting a sea of measurements, they deduced which environmental factors control chlorophyll levels in surface waters. The analysis links the ocean's greenness, and its productivity, to the conditions that set it.
plos-pone-0003936: In 2008, Cahu, Olichon, and Hentrich caught a cell-division motor getting its grip. Phosphorylation by Cdk1 boosted how tightly the Eg5 motor binds microtubules. The tighter binding, seen in test tubes and frog egg extracts, powers spindle assembly. The result shows a chemical tag switching a molecular motor into high gear.
plos-pone-0004036: In 2008, D'Agata, Dupont-Rouzeyrol, and Magal tested how drug schedules breed resistance. Different antibiotic regimens were compared for how fast resistant bacteria emerged. The choice of drug regimen shaped the rise of antimicrobial-resistant strains. The results guide prescribing to slow one of medicine's gravest threats.
plos-pone-0004136: In 2009, Xia and Holcik found floppy RNA working the hardest. Strong eukaryotic IRES elements carried weak secondary RNA structure. The looser the RNA fold, the better ribosomes hopped aboard. The neat rule simplifies the hunt for hidden gene-start switches.
plos-pone-0004236: In 2009, Mruk and Kobertz found a new key for heart channels. They discovered an activator of KCNQ1-KCNE1 potassium channel complexes. The compound tuned the channels' gating. The tool aids heart-rhythm drug research. The activator helps probe how KCNE partners shape currents.
plos-pone-0004336: In 2009, Rizzoli, Hauffe, and Tagliapietra linked deer to brain-fever risk. Forest structure and roe deer abundance predicted tick-borne encephalitis risk in Italy. The deer-rich woods harbored more risk. The model guides prevention. The work maps where the virus threat runs hottest.
plos-pone-0358136: Vaccines only work when they are given correctly. This observational study assessed vaccination competency among health workers in health facilities in East Wollega, Oromia, Western Ethiopia. The competency gaps it found show exactly where training must go to protect every link in the immunization chain.
plos-pone-0357836: ANCA-associated vasculitis can roar back even during rituximab maintenance therapy. This single-center retrospective cohort studied clinical outcomes after relapse on rituximab-based maintenance. The outcomes data help doctors plan the next move when the maintenance strategy fails a patient.
plos-pone-0358536: American Indian and Alaska Native youth face devastating rates of suicide and self-harm. This paper published a protocol for a systematic review of risk factors and methods of self-injury and suicide attempts in this population. The advance-published plan sets up rigorous evidence that could directly save young lives.
plos-pone-0350236: Farm sensors need power without the hassle of batteries. This paper designed ambient RF energy harvesting using a voltage doubler rectifier for battery-free agricultural sensor networks — complete with statistical analysis and machine learning validation. The harvester sips stray radio waves to keep field sensors running indefinitely.
plos-pone-0358036: Elite women’s soccer demands exquisitely precise load management. This paper built a temporally validated and calibrated monitoring framework that prioritizes next-day readiness decline, using readiness, workload, and wellness data. The system tells coaches which players are truly ready — and which ones need rest before they break.
plos-pone-0321836: How do people around the world perceive the risk of the climate crisis? This paper developed and validated the global climate crisis risk perception scale (GCCRP-S). The rigorously tested tool lets researchers measure climate dread across cultures — and compare it meaningfully.
plos-pone-0347436: When TB tests come back negative but clinical suspicion runs high, treating empirically saves lives. This Ugandan study examined empiric tuberculosis treatment and 12-month mortality among sputum GeneXpert-negative adults living with HIV. The findings support treating on clinical grounds in the antiretroviral therapy era.
plos-pone-0356236: Talking in noise makes us shout — the Lombard effect — and Mandarin Chinese has its own signature. This paper compared spectro-temporal versus purely spectral features for predicting the Lombard gain in Mandarin. The winning features reveal how tonal languages adapt to noise.
plos-pone-0354736: Black locust trees — Robinia pseudoacacia — grow very differently uphill versus down. This study identified altitudinal and slope gradients as key determinants of the species’ growth. The findings help foresters plant this fast-growing tree where it will actually thrive.
plos-pone-0355236: Charging devices underwater without cables sounds like science fiction. This paper developed and experimentally validated a composite rod underwater acoustic wireless charging system. Using sound waves to transmit power through water, the system could one day keep subsea sensors and vehicles running indefinitely. The successful validation proves the physics works outside the lab.
plos-pone-0353836: Borderline personality disorder patients often wait months for therapy — online psychoeducation could bridge the gap. This pilot study assessed the safety, feasibility, and mechanisms of online psychoeducation and assessment as a first step of care. The promising results suggest digital first steps can safely start the healing sooner.
plos-pone-0355936: Diroximel fumarate — an MS drug — may protect the nervous system through immune calming. This paper showed it confers neuroprotection via reduced Th1 responses and induction of the anti-oxidative Nrf2 pathway in experimental neuroinflammation. The dual mechanism deepens our understanding of a drug already in patients’ hands.
plos-pone-0356536: Fashion designers are meeting generative AI — with fascination and fear. This paper explored their acceptance of AIGC through a dual-pathway stimulus–organism–response analysis. The findings reveal what draws designers toward AI tools and what repels them — essential intelligence for the industry’s creative future.
plos-pone-0355836: Hospital patients receiving physical or occupational therapy hope to leave functioning as before. This paper examined the factors associated with returning to pre-admission functional category at discharge among acute inpatients. The findings help therapists predict who’ll recover independence — and who needs more intensive rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0351836: Indonesia can eliminate tuberculosis — with the right regimen economics. This paper catalyzed that conversation with health economic and policy insights on the BPaL regimen. The analysis shows shorter, all-oral MDR-TB treatment isn’t just clinically superior — it’s economically transformative.
europmc-pmc2815736: Exercise and diet send molecular signals through muscle, and this 2009 paper traces one important chain. The authors show these signals regulate SIRT3 and switch on AMPK and PGC-1alpha in skeletal muscle, pathways tied to energy use. The work connects lifestyle to the cell's energy machinery. It helped explain, at the molecular level, why exercise keeps metabolism healthy.
europmc-pmc2835736: Evolutionary trees from huge alignments take forever to compute, so this 2010 paper offers a shortcut. The authors introduce FastTree 2, which builds approximately maximum-likelihood trees for large datasets quickly. They show it scales where older methods stall. The program became essential for big phylogenetic studies.
europmc-pmc2841636: U.S. hives swam in farm sprays, this 2010 count found. The team gauged mite-killers and crop sprays in hives coast to coast and weighed what they mean for bee health. Their tally bared a dose few had sized up. The find recast bee loss as partly a poisoning problem.
europmc-pmc2854736: Soft plastics shed phthalates that reach the womb, and this 2010 study tracks the kids. The team tied womb contact to child conduct and thinking-control scores. Their read linked the compounds to restless, rash acts. The tie fed the push to curb the compounds in kids' goods.
europmc-pmc2882336: Online therapy for depression needs a human touch, but whose? This 2010 trial compares internet depression treatment with clinician versus technician support. The authors test whether expert help beats trained aides for outcomes. Their result shaped how digital therapy programs are staffed and scaled.
europmc-pmc2892436: The beloved R-squared can mislead for curved models. This 2010 paper evaluates R2 as an inadequate measure for nonlinear models in drug and biochemistry research, using Monte Carlo tests. The authors show its failure plainly. Their warning steered analysts to better fits.
europmc-pmc2908536: Tumors shed tiny bubbles that disarm immunity. This 2010 paper shows tumor-made microvesicles grow regulatory T cells and boost their muting power. The authors reveal a stealth weapon of cancer. Their finding explains part of how tumors dodge the immune system.
europmc-pmc2936536: High-altitude peoples adapted to thin air, and this 2010 paper finds the genes behind it. The authors scan Tibetan and Andean genomes for marks of natural selection. Their dense scans reveal altitude-tuned genes. The work illuminates human adaptation at its most extreme.
europmc-pmc2956736: Sequencing data needs a quick health check. This 2010 paper introduces SolexaQA for at-a-glance quality assessment of Illumina sequencing data. The authors' tool spots bad runs fast. Their software became a QC staple. Labs run it before trusting any read set.
europmc-pmc2984136: A grain mold toxin threatens food safety worldwide. This 2010 review covers deoxynivalenol, the vomitoxin, and its harms. The authors survey where it strikes and how. Their overview informs grain safety rules. Pigs refuse tainted feed, a telltale sign. Millers test every harvest for the toxin.
europmc-pmc3002336: Blood microRNAs might flag cancer early. This 2010 paper reviews tiny blood RNAs as no-cut biomarkers for cancer. The authors survey the early promise. Their overview points to future blood tests. One vial could screen for many tumors. The field is still proving the signals.
europmc-pmc3075236: Snakebites kill tens of thousands in India. This 2011 survey counts snakebite deaths across India. The authors' national numbers demand action. Their work spurred antivenom drives. Rural farmers face the deadliest risk. The toll rivaled better-known killers. Antivenom stockpiles grew after the count.
europmc-pmc3091536: Dutch pandemic fears got measured. This 2011 paper surveys Dutch risk perception and behavior in early H1N1 days. The authors reveal the public mood. Their work guides risk communication. Most people stayed calm, they found. Clear messages beat scary ones.
europmc-pmc3101336: Oxidant stress got a pregnancy review. This 2011 paper reviews oxidant stress across pregnancy's stages. The authors survey the evidence. Their overview guides baby doctors. Too much stress threatens the placenta. Antioxidant trials showed mixed results. The review steers prenatal research.
europmc-pmc6506336: Scientists exposed 324 lab-grown human stem cells to 79 known or suspected cancer-causing chemicals and mapped the DNA damage each one left behind. The result is a reference catalog of "mutational signatures" - telltale mutation patterns that point back to specific causes. Doctors and researchers can use it to figure out what triggered a tumor by reading its genome.
europmc-pmc6511336: Medicines only work if people take them, and millions of patients with long-term illness do not. This paper reviews dozens of reviews to map out why - cost, side effects, forgetfulness, beliefs about treatment, and more. By pulling the big picture together, it shows doctors and policymakers where to aim their efforts to help patients stick with their prescriptions.
europmc-pmc6566436: Plants cannot run from threats, so they signal: jasmonic acid is a hormone that rallies defenses against chewing insects and wounding, while also steering growth. This review maps the jasmonate signaling pathway - how the signal is made, read, and acted on. The circuitry reveals how plants balance growing against defending.
europmc-pmc6573036: We breathe plastic: indoor air carries tiny microplastic fibers and fragments, but how much do we actually inhale? Researchers used a breathing thermal manikin - a life-size dummy that inhales like a human - to measure exposure. The first-of-its-kind test puts numbers on an invisible pollutant we all live with.
europmc-pmc6582336: Sorting genomes into populations - who belongs with whom - gets slow as datasets balloon. Fastbaps is a speedy statistical tool that clusters DNA samples into genetic groups using Bayesian math, handling huge collections in a fraction of the usual time. Population geneticists get fast, principled answers about structure in their data.
europmc-pmc6598536: PEG-coated drug carriers were assumed to be immunologically invisible - a stealth cloak for nanomedicine. Not so: this review documents the immune responses PEGylated liposomes can trigger, including rapid clearance by anti-PEG antibodies. The findings force drug designers to reckon with the immune system's memory of a supposedly inert coating.
europmc-pmc6624636: Akkermansia muciniphila - a gut bacterium linked to leanness - may also calm inflamed bowels. This study tested two strains in mice with chronic colitis, finding strain-specific anti-inflammatory effects. Not all probiotic strains are equal, and the work shows why strain-level testing matters before health claims.
europmc-pmc6659036: Inside tumors, T cells wear down - exhausted by endless antigen exposure. This review charts T cell dysfunction in cancer: the brakes that get stuck on, and how immunotherapy tries to release them. Reviving tired T cells remains the central challenge of cancer immune therapy.
europmc-pmc6675736: Plasmodium vivax - the relapsing malaria - has been hard to map, until now. This study modeled its global reach from 2000 to 2017 in space and time. The maps show where vivax persists and where it retreats, guiding elimination campaigns against a stubborn foe.
europmc-pmc6694136: Long life runs in families - but which genes carry the gift? Pooling genome-wide studies of over 11,000 exceptionally long-lived people, this meta-analysis hunted longevity genes. The harvest: multiple DNA variants tied to surviving past the 90th percentile of lifespan.
europmc-pmc6731336: Aging and diabetes damage the same organs through eerily similar routes - and zombie cells may be the link. This review places cellular senescence at the nexus: senescent cells pile up with age and obesity, driving dysfunction. Clearing these retirees could treat both aging and diabetes at once.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-36: GAO warned Congress in 2007 that a bad flu wave would test the crews who keep power, water, and phones alive — and that no joint plan existed. Guarding those lifelines needs government and private firms rowing as one, but GAO found the rowing badly out of sync. The report urges the two sides to plan together before a crisis does the planning for them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1036: Hackers were eyeing the computers that run power plants and factories — and GAO's 2007 report says the defense was a work in progress. Plenty of shield programs were rolling, but the holes stayed real. The findings map a race the nation was not yet winning: locking down the industrial brains before someone else reached them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-936: The Army's new-look brigades needed a training doctrine to match in 2007 — GAO's report says the modular-force game plan was half-written. The findings press the service to finish the playbook for its reshaped combat teams. Reorganized troops, the report warns, still need a coherent school.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-836: Drones were crowding the skies in 2007 — GAO's report says the Pentagon needed better coordination and visibility to get the most from unmanned aircraft. The findings call for joined-up drone doctrine. The report's vision: robot wings working as one fleet, not a flock of solo acts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-536: Homeland Security's money systems stayed tangled in 2007 — GAO's report says the department-wide finance merger remained a stubborn challenge. The findings describe the accounting knot left by the rushed mega-merger. The report's refrain: merged departments need merged books, or the numbers never add up.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-736: The 2010 address hunt was improving in 2007 — GAO's report says the Census Bureau's local address update had gotten better, with challenges left. The findings credit the progress and flag the gaps. The report treats every missed address as a missed American.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-336: The Energy Department's mega-projects needed a readiness yardstick in 2007 — GAO's report says a consistent way to judge new technology was missing. The findings demand the measure. The report's lesson: bet big on tech only after the tech proves itself.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-236: Disability aid was a bureaucratic maze in 2007, and GAO's report says stronger federal oversight could assure the programs' accountability. The findings demand the watch. The report warns that the many helping hands needed one firm grip. The maze needed a map.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-36: The nuclear weapons complex needed better management in 2007, and GAO's report says more action was required to run the nation's atomic enterprise. The findings demand the discipline. The report warns that the arsenal's stewards needed tighter hands. The bombs' keepers needed watching.
openalex-w7208837836: Brazil's federal institutes were created to give working-class students free technical and higher education. This study reviews academic research on how free-market economic policies have reshaped that mission. Drawing on a systematic review of graduate-level research, the authors map how market-driven reforms affect curricula, funding, and the public role of these schools. It asks whether the original goal of serving workers and communities is surviving.
openalex-w7204954936: The most dangerous hack often starts with a convincing lie. This paper studies social engineering, manipulating people rather than machines, as both a crime trend and a tool for police intelligence in Para. The authors trace how digital life made human gullibility a prime target for fraud, then examine the applications and legal limits of using these techniques in police work. A sober look at the human weak point in cybersecurity.
openalex-w7204966536: A burst stomach ulcer is a surgical emergency, and surgeons can fix it two ways: open surgery or keyhole surgery through small cuts. This paper compares how patients do after each method, looking at healing, problems, and survival. The authors pull together the evidence as keyhole repair gains ground on the older open approach. A practical comparison for emergency teams that must choose fast.
openalex-w7204852936: Mental health is moving to the center of education debates, and this article maps why. The authors study how the well-being of teachers and students shapes teaching and learning, in both directions. Drawing on current research, they trace the links between a healthy mind and a working classroom. A timely overview for schools realizing that no lesson plan survives a mental health crisis.
openalex-w7205007036: In February 2026, Brazil's health agency created the country's first general federal rules for companies growing cannabis for medical use. This article asks what the new regulation really changed, moving from a history of prohibition to national production. The authors parse the resolutions and their practical effects. Essential reading for anyone following how medical cannabis went from banned to regulated in Brazil.
openalex-w7155037536: Programs linking high schools with universities may inspire future doctors. This exploratory study tested whether such a collaboration boosted learning drive and career understanding among aspiring medical students in Japan. The authors measured the motivational effects. An education study of planting medical ambitions early.
pmc-13467436: In this 2026 neuroscience paper, researchers found that short-term depression of signal strength in the hippocampal CA1 region — a memory hub of the brain — can occur without calcium. Since calcium was thought to drive this weakening of synapses, the calcium-independent path is a notable twist. It adds a new piece to how memory circuits adjust their strength.
pmc-13471736: A 2026 computational chemistry paper optimizing random phase approximation calculations — a high-accuracy quantum method — for energies of molecules, solids, and surfaces. Faster, cheaper RPA calculations mean better predictions of how materials behave without lab experiments. The optimizations make a powerful method practical for everyday use.
pmc-13458036: A 2026 cancer immunology paper showing that CD155, a protein made by tumor cells themselves, reprograms cancer metabolism through the PI3K/AKT/HIF-1α glycolysis pathway — and that this reprogramming makes lung tumors resist anti-PD-1 immunotherapy. Blocking the metabolic escape route could restore the drugs' power for patients who stop responding.
pmc-13448136: A 2026 cancer paper showing that the SLC7A5 transporter helps colorectal cancer spread to the liver by rewiring tryptophan metabolism through the kynurenine/XANA–AhR pathway and reshaping the immune microenvironment. Tumors hijack this metabolic route to disarm nearby immunity. Blocking the transporter could slow metastasis.
pmc-13433836: A 2026 review on amino acid homeostasis in the kidney — how the organ balances these building blocks — covering normal physiology and what goes wrong in disease. The kidney is central to amino acid metabolism, and the paper maps both sides. It serves nephrologists and biochemists alike.
pmc-13425036: A 2026 systematic review of predictive models for motor outcomes after deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease. DBS helps many but not all, and predicting who benefits would transform patient selection. The review assesses which models are actually ready for the clinic.
pmc-13419936: A 2026 study finding that alternate-day fasting has sex-specific anti-inflammatory effects in middle-aged rats, acting through TLR4 and leptin signaling. Males and females responded differently to the same fasting regimen. The result is a reminder that nutrition research must account for sex.
pmc-13439936: In this 2026 C. elegans paper, the mid-pachytene transition between early and late double-strand breaks in meiosis proved conserved through early adulthood and coincided with a key regulatory shift (the title is truncated). Meiotic timing is tightly controlled. The conservation finding underscores its importance.
pmc-13475236: This 2026 data paper presented an ancient Bengal numismatic dataset — coinage of Vanga, Gauda, Samatata, and Harikela. The coins record early South Asian history. The dataset is a resource for historians.
